L19: ## house-of-fishing
L20: 
L21: by 【16†hattorihanzo1111】 / 【17†rawpayload】
L22: 
L23: Rating:
L24: TL;DR
L25: Leakless glibc-2.39 exploit on a heap-style chal whose only primitives are create/update/delete/copy (with no offset, no overflow, no read). The win condition is *admin == 0xdeadbeefdeadcafe where admin points to a fixed mmap'd page at 0x1337000. Solution chains a largebin attack to plant a heap pointer at *(0x1337008), then a tcache stash unlink through a fake chunk header at 0x1336FF0 so that tcache_put writes entries[bin] = 0x1337000 directly.
L26: The next malloc(0x90) returns the admin page; we write the magic value and trigger the hidden case 5 to call system("/bin/sh").
L27: 【18†Original writeup†blog.rawpayload.com】 (https://blog.rawpayload.com/blog/trx-ctf-2026-house-of-fishing-writeup).

L19: ## down-the-line
L20: 
L21: by 【16†hattorihanzo1111】 / 【17†rawpayload】
L22: 
L23: Rating:
L24: 
L25: Summary
L26: chall.bin is a 16-bit x86 boot sector served through QEMU. The service exposes a tiny allocator with three menu actions:
L27: 
L28: allocate a chunk
L29: edit a chunk
L30: print a chunk to a selected I/O port
L31: The flag is not in the loaded boot sector. It is appended in the second disk sector, so the exploit has to make the guest read from disk.
L32: 
L33: Final flag:
L34: 
L35: TRX{d0wn_7h3_a20_l1n3_f7w}

L19: ## slop_allocator
L20: 
L21: by 【16†hattorihanzo1111】 / 【17†rawpayload】
L22: 
L23: Rating:
L24: 
L25: The challenge
L26: A NASA-themed memory-management simulator in C. The user manages "spaceships" (structs of permission + char *notes[16]) and "notes" (variable-size blobs), all served by a custom slab/page allocator called SLOP. The menu offers:
L27: allocate spaceship
L28: allocate note (under a chosen ship+slot, with caller-chosen length)
L29: free note
L30: takeoff (prints the spaceship pointer if permission != 0)
L31: anything else → exit(1)
L32: The binary is full RELRO, PIE, canary, NX, plus IBT and shadow stack. Linked against glibc 2.41 (the docker uses ubuntu:25.04).
L33:

L19: ## faulty-road
L20: 
L21: by 【16†hattorihanzo1111】 / 【17†rawpayload】
L22: 
L23: Rating:
L24: 
L25: The final reliable recovery path was:
L26: Reverse driver.ko and identify where the flag lives in the loaded kernel module.
L27: Use the unstable physical-page corruption exploit until it drops us into a root shell.
L28: Do not execute another uploaded ELF after root, because the exploit has already damaged kernel/page-cache state.
L29: Use BusyBox shell tools to read the loaded module memory through /proc/kcore.
L30: Extract the string from the live flag symbol in driver.ko's .data section.
L31: The important loaded-module fact is:
L32: driver.ko:.data + 0x170 == flag
L33: On the remote instance, /proc/kallsyms exposed the live flag [driver] address after root, and reading that address from /proc/kcore produced the flag.
L34:
